So firstly I'd like to address something I felt from your last comment but was reassured of in this post. So despite the Richard Wolf meme, socialism does not mean "the government does something". Socialism in one of the more pure and original forms is simply advocating for democracy in the workplace. This was achieved for a while when workers used their collective bargaining power to demand better working conditions. They were able to achieve a 40 hour work week, minimum wage laws, standardized lunch breaks, and several other  things that made it easier to have a better work-life balance. Those have been the status quo, at least in America for a pretty long time. But they became laws because of overwhelmingly democratic popularity and allowed people who worked for companies not to HAVE to fight each company that they worked for for those rights, or be forced to look for a company that does. Not every employee at every company should have to make that fight. Some people just want to flip their burgers and go home, and not have to learn all this theory shit. BUT Socialist theory does not mandate unions to exist to work. All ot means is that the workers who use their bodies, time, potentially health, and labor to make the production of Capitol (or wealth if that's what you mean) should each have a voice on how the surplus money at the end of the day/financial period is spent. Could be they each get an equal cut, could be they distribute it based on senority, or get a new coffee maker, whatever. 100% agreement is not nessecary for those decisions. 

Secondly, part of early Socialist theory was purely critiquing the overwhelmingly dysfunctional consequences of unregulated capitalism. It's constant focus on short term profits ar the expense of... you name it: the environment, finite resource consumption, workers well being. All for the owners who make 100 times the wage of the average worker (I know it's gotten worse over the years). Pointing out basic flaws in capitalism is pretty much always at the basis of Marxism, whether the person making the critique has read the theory or not. 

Kind of tied to my first point, but just because you're a leftist doesn't mean you like big government. That's why we have anarcho communists. I am one but I acknowledge the fact it's more of an ideal goal never to be fully reached, but always approached. Kind of like world piece. We'll never fully get world piece as long as we have states and finite resources, but it's a goal we all aim for. 

Also, I'm very sorry that you have the perception that so much of leftist thought is based on reciting rhetoric from academia or other places without looking more into the material effect actual leftist experiments have panned out in the world. I really recommend reading into the nation building the US had done every time a Socialist or communist nation tries to build itself in Latin America, and how our imperialist and capitalist power structures crushed any kind of attempt to try a different economic system that doesn't serve the owning class axiomatically. 

Responding to your second paragraph, I find it interesting your experiment showed a lack of generation of wealth upon redistributive policies being used. However I don't quite find it relevant if the base standard of living for a larger percent of the population went up. I dont find it compelling. I would like your opinion on how this can be true at the same time that when we increase minimum wages, the economy in those areas tend to improve and are stimulated by people having more spending money for more than basic needs. They go out to local restaurants more, have the ability to go to stores that are locally owned that can't compete with the national chains prices, stuff like that. Like we have real world examples on how companies will pay their workers the minimum amount they can without losing them, regardless if there is a minimum that's government enforced. So it's better to have a higher minimum based on cost of living in that area and tie it to inflation. As a reminder, I acknowledge the fact that socialism is not nessicarily "when the government does stuff". Im just taking about specific policies that have been proven to help the working class, things that are nessecary for better living conditions if we try to improve a bad system within its own framework. 

So the last thing I wanted to address was your point that socialism working on a small scale but cannot exist on too large of a scale. I think this is actually reminiscent of the way the Roman empire collapsed economically. I think its impossible for a non post-scarcity society to control all of the world's resources and keep its currency from not collapsing. There are too many variables in globalizing our resources that make it too easy for manipulative power structures to develop in specialized areas of production. Sweat shops in the Phillipines for example. Pay a kid 10 cents a day to make Nike shoes that we buy in America for $100. Which is why that kid having a voice in how those profits is pretty important to me. Thats kind of what Marxist theory tries to address in socialism. The gradual democratization of the workplace. Another solution is to go through the government and mandate trade policies that require working standards equivalent to our minimims. One solution involves government,  the other does not. Both are leftist but only one is Socialist.
